item.title: Physical Learning for Autonomous Tuning of Spin Qubits in Electrostatically Defined Quantum Dots
item.description:
Read new method — Multiplexed gradient descent on an FPGA local controller continuously tracks drift up to 0.3 mV/s and recovers from discrete jumps up to 1 mV in 0.7 s (330 iterations), holding within a 134 μV tolerance without prior knowledge of the cross-capacitance matrix.

Grade 0.600 · 4.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Colloquium : Advances in automation of quantum dot devices control”

Asks

How can electrostatically defined quantum dots be autonomously stabilized at target idling and pulsing points without repeating full charge-stability diagram scans or relying on model-dependent feedback loops?

Before

Continuous stabilization required periodic 2D scans taking seconds followed by neural-network and Hough transform inference, or monotonic single-peak PID loops that diverge under cross-capacitance.

But

Quantum dot and charge noise simulated rather than physically measured on-chip. Pulsing point assumes both virtual-gate directions are constrained, which requires two SETs in physical implementation.

Tools

multiplexed gradient descent (MGD) · simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) · FPGA-in-the-loop controller · simulated double quantum dot and SET sensor

Abstract

Tuning electrostatically defined quantum dots remains a primary bottleneck in the scalability of semiconductor spin qubits. While existing solutions rely on machine learning algorithms, these approaches require global information, introduce latency bottlenecks, and tax the limited cooling power available at cryogenic stages. Here, we demonstrate an FPGA-in-the-loop learning paradigm that bypasses digital computing overhead by utilizing multiplexed gradient descent (MGD) for tuning. Implemented on an FPGA and an emulated quantum dot device, our system autonomously tracks environmental drift, dynamically recovers from discrete charge jumps, and maintains steady-state stabilization in low signal-to-noise ratio regimes, without prior knowledge of the device's cross-capacitance matrix. The system also navigates the charge-stability landscape to stabilize the quantum dot around optimal operating points. These results demonstrate a ``compute-in-place'' platform, with a logic and power footprint suited to future cryo-CMOS integration, that provides autonomous stabilization of quantum dots at desired operating points, creating an auto-tuning system for spin qubits that is resilient to electrostatic drifts, changing noise profiles, and two-level fluctuations.
